analysis.one_liner: Approves the Keystone XL oil pipeline without a presidential permit.
analysis.headline: The bill to approve the Keystone XL pipeline was placed on the Senate calendar but never debated or voted on before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have Congress directly approve TransCanada's application to build the northern Keystone XL pipeline from Canada to Nebraska, eliminating the need for a presidential permit. It would also declare the 2011 State Department environmental review complete, cutting off any further environmental study. It would leave Nebraska's own work on the in-state portion of the route untouched.
analysis.who_benefits: TransCanada, which filed the pipeline application in May 2012, would gain immediate approval and skip the presidential permitting process and any further environmental review. Canadian oil sands producers and refiners would gain a dedicated route to move heavy Canadian crude to Gulf Coast refineries. Construction firms and workers on the project would gain the jobs the pipeline build-out would create.
analysis.who_benefits_short: TransCanada and Canadian oil sands producers

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that no presidential permit is required for TransCanada's May 4, 2012 application for the pipeline from the Canadian border to the South Dakota/Nebraska border, immediately advancing the project without executive approval.

It deems the final environmental impact statement the Secretary of State issued in August 2011 to satisfy all requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act, ending further federal environmental review of the pipeline.
It preserves Nebraska's ongoing state-level work on the portion of the pipeline entirely within Nebraska, allowing that routing dispute to continue separately.

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the risks the bill would foreclose review of: potential pipeline spills, including over the Ogallala Aquifer in Nebraska, and the climate effects of moving oil sands crude to market. Landowners along the route bear eminent-domain easements. The bill also removes a check that normally rests with the President on cross-border infrastructure, concentrating the decision in Congress for this one company's project.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities along the route and the public

drawbacks.text: By declaring the 2011 environmental review sufficient, the bill would cut off any new study of spill risks, water impacts, or climate effects before construction began.

It would override the long-standing executive process under which the President decides whether to permit pipelines that cross the national border, moving that decision to Congress for a single project.
Even supporters acknowledged the Nebraska routing dispute over the aquifer was unresolved; the bill only exempts that piece from its approval rather than resolving it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a clear, immediate gain to one company and the oil sands industry by shortcutting both presidential permitting and environmental review. The costs are diffuse and long-term: unreviewed spill risk over a major aquifer, added carbon emissions, and a precedent for Congress approving individual infrastructure projects by name. An honest weighing finds the benefits concentrated and the risks unexamined by design.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar within two days of introduction, but it was never debated or voted on, and it died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. John Hoeven introduced the bill in the Senate on September 20, 2012, with three Republican cosponsors.
Within two days it had been read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 533.
No committee referral, debate, or vote followed; the action record ends there, and the bill expired when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of the expedited pipeline approval came out ahead: because the bill never passed, the decision on TransCanada's permit stayed where it had been, with the executive branch, and no further environmental review was cut off by statute. TransCanada gained nothing from this bill.

for.name: Sen. John Hoeven
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to approve the Keystone XL pipeline without a presidential permit.

for.name: Sens. Richard Lugar, David Vitter, and Lisa Murkowski
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's original cosponsors; three additional Republican senators cosponsored it.

against.name: Senate Democratic leadership
against.role: Senate Majority Leader and caucus controlling the floor
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for debate or a vote, leaving it on the calendar until the Congress ended.

against.name: Environmental and landowner opponents of Keystone XL
against.role: National environmental groups and Nebraska landowners
against.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned against fast-tracking the pipeline, citing spill risk over the Ogallala Aquifer and climate effects of oil sands crude, raising the political cost of moving the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democratic senator signed on; the bill died on the calendar under a Democratic-controlled Senate.

industries.note: The bill would hand the company statutory approval of its May 2012 application, skipping the presidential permit and further environmental review entirely. Its gain comes from avoiding the review process ordinary communities rely on to contest spills and land takings.

A completed Keystone XL would give oil sands crude a direct pipeline route to Gulf Coast refineries, expanding production capacity. The bill's approval advances that market access while foreclosing environmental review of the consequences.

Refiners equipped to process heavy Canadian crude would gain a cheaper, dedicated supply line. Some benefit could pass through to fuel consumers, but the bill's design directs the benefit to the shippers first.
Rail has carried much of the oil sands output that a pipeline would displace, so a legislated approval would take that business away. Consumers see little difference either way in this bill's terms.
